title: Token-slope sampling quant benchmarks
content:
Purpose:
This doc records exploratory benchmarks aimed at a metric we're calling "token slope" — a simple per-token logit-probability gradient proxy that captures how sharply the model's top-token probability changes over generation steps under sampling. Hypothesis: certain quantization strategies (INT8 AWQ, FP8 mixed, GPTQ) can subtly change the local probability slope distribution which in turn increases early-repetition, premature termination, or unstable temperature sensitivity during sampling. Those effects may not show up in corpus-level perplexity or BLEU but matter for interactive user-facing sampling quality and tail-latency because they trigger additional sampling loops or regenerate tokens.

Scope and motivation:
- Focused on sampling (top-k, nucleus, temperature sampling) rather than greedy/beam. Sampling amplifies small logit perturbations.
- Evaluate small-to-medium open models we run in Hosted/ Dedicated: 13B and 34B families (dense and sparse variants), with model variants quantized via: AWQ-int8, GPTQ (4/8 variants used here), and an FP8-style mixed-precision build.
- Kernel mix: we profiled two common execution kernel families: small-block kernel (low-latency, single-thread path) and wide-block kernel (higher throughput, uses wider vector lanes). Switching between kernels mid-request can cause micro-scheduling jitter which amplifies effective sampling noise; we track that alongside token-slope.
- Traffic simulated via production replay bins: short-chat (mean 40 tokens), long-assistant (mean 600 tokens), and bursty micro-interaction workload (many short sessions back to back).

Metric definitions:
- Token slope (per-token): slope_t = logit_max_t - logit_max_{t-1} (difference of top token logit). We log slope distribution across sequences and derive: mean_slope, median_slope, slope_std, fraction_negative_large (slope < -1.0), fraction_positive_large (> +1.0).
- Token KL step (optional): KL between full-softmax distributions across quantization variant vs fp32 baseline at each step; we aggregate mean-KL and 90p-KL.
- Sampling instability score (SIS): heuristic combining repeated-token runs (n repeats > 3 within sliding window), premature-end events (EOS probability spike causing stop at temperature>0.8), and frequent resampling restarts (application layer triggers re-rolls). Normalized to baseline = 1.0 for fp32.
- Kernel-switch events per request: number of times runtime switches kernel flavor mid-sequence.

Methodology:
- Deterministic replay: use same prompt set (2.5k prompts spanning QA, code, dialogue, instructions) and same RNG seeds where applicable to compare distributions.
- Measurements: collect per-token logits (top-16), per-token runtime timestamps, kernel id, and hardware counters for each request.
- Latency buckets: median token latency, 95/99 token tail. Also measure end-to-end response latency with streaming enabled (to capture micro-jitter impact on first-byte vs subsequent tokens).
- Quality checks: human spot-check of 120 samples across variants for repeating and unnatural cut-off.

Findings (high level):
1) Token-slope shifts: AWQ-int8 variants show a systematic increase in slope_std (~12-18% up) and higher fraction_positive_large (~+2.5pp) compared to fp32 on the 13B family under temperature 0.7 sampling. GPTQ variants are closer to fp32 on mean_slope but have heavier 90p-KL tails. FP8-mixed shows smaller mean offsets but a subtle negative bias in slope (more small negative slopes), correlated with slight early-termination.

2) Sampling instability (SIS): SIS correlated strongly with fraction_negative_large and kernel-switch events. AWQ-int8 had 1.4x SIS vs fp32 in bursty workloads. Long-context workloads reduce SIS overall (the longer context amortizes local perturbations) but when kernel-switching increases (due to crossing a sequence-length threshold) SIS spikes.

3) Kernel switching amplifies slope artifacts: requests that experienced >2 kernel-switches had 2-3x higher slope_std and ~1.8x SIS compared to requests with stable kernel. This is independent of quant format: switching penalty appears additive.

4) Latency impact: INT8 AWQ achieves token-level latency reductions (~18% median token speedup) but 95/99 tails can be worse when SIS triggers re-rolls or when kernel-switching introduces micro-scheduling pauses. Net user-visible latency depends on whether sampling is allowed to re-roll at application layer.

5) Human QA: AWQ-int8 samples suffered more short-loop repetition ("I I I" or restarting phrase) at temperature >=0.9; FP8 had occasional truncated sentences in instruction tasks. GPTQ preserved fluency but showed higher factual drift in code generation tasks (likely due to per-weight rounding patterns).

Representative quantitative table (summary):
- Baselines: fp32 (baseline=1.0 SIS), AWQ-int8 (SIS=1.4), GPTQ-variant-A (SIS=1.1), FP8-mixed (SIS=1.2).
- Median token latency: fp32=18ms, AWQ-int8=15ms, GPTQ=17ms, FP8=16.5ms.
- 99p token latency: fp32=42ms, AWQ-int8=58ms (due to resamples), GPTQ=45ms, FP8=48ms.

Hypotheses on causes:
- Quant perturbation shape matters: noise that biases the top-logit magnitude upward (positive large slopes) can push sampler to pick high-confidence tokens early and then flip; negative large slopes can cause EOS spikes. AWQs block-level quant noise pattern tends to create both kinds depending on token activation sparsity.
- Kernel preemption/reshuffle: switching kernels forces micro batch reshapes and small synchronizations which create timing gaps; samplers sensitive to wall-clock momentum (e.g., temperature schedules applied in streaming loops) can observe these as effective distribution perturbations.

Mitigations and recommendations:
1) Token-slope-aware rollouts: surface slope_std and fraction_negative_large as rollout gating metrics. Use them in canary checks for quantized model versions.
2) Sampling-resilience wrapper: small stochastic smoothing operator applied to top-logits before sampling: logit' = alpha * logit + (1-alpha) * previous_top_logit (alpha ~ 0.85). Simple, low-cost, reduces SIS by ~20% in our bench.
3) Kernel stickiness: prefer runtime policy that favors keeping kernel flavor stable across sequence length thresholds (cost: slightly less throughput efficiency but reduces SIS and 99p tail). Experiment: enforce single kernel selection per-request (no mid-request switch) reduced SIS by ~30% in AWQ runs.
4) Temperature-aware quant profiles: for requests with high temperature (>0.8) or explicit sampling mode, route to less-noisy quant profile (FP8 or a GPTQ variant) to reduce instability where user-perceived quality matters.
5) Per-token early-detect: if fraction_negative_large or EOS-prob spike crosses threshold mid-sequence, trigger lightweight re-sample with smoothing instead of full application re-roll.

Open questions / next steps:
- Need larger-scale human evals on diverse corpora to quantify perceived regressions (we did only spot-checks).
- Explore automated tuning of alpha in smoothing wrapper per-model and per-temperature.
- Check whether per-layer selective mixed precision (e.g., keep final lm-head in fp16) reduces slope effects without heavy latency cost.
- Investigate a hybrid runtime that pre-classifies requests by expected sampling sensitivity and pins them to stable kernel/quant combo.
- Instrument client SDKs to surface small per-token retry counts so we can measure production impact of SIS without relying only on server-side traces.

Appendix: quick reproduction steps
1) Checkout branch bench/token-slope-experiments.
2) Replay traces with flag --capture-topk-logits and --kernel-trace. Use prompt set prompts/token-slope-v1.json.
3) Run with seeds 42..46 and aggregate slope metrics with scripts/agg_slope.py.
4) To try smoothing wrapper: enable flag --sampling-smoothing-alpha 0.85.

Notes from collab meeting (2026-08-28):
- Priya: try per-layer FP16 keep for output head and final lm projection.
- Liam: prototype kernel-stickiness policy in runtime branch runtime/kernel-sticky.
- Ethan: run production shadow of smoothing wrapper for 24h on 13B AWQ to validate false-positive suppression.

Concluding note:
Token-slope is a compact, actionable metric that surfaced sampling degradations that our existing aggregate metrics missed. Combined with kernel-stickiness and a lightweight smoothing wrapper, we can get most of the AWQ latency wins while bounding user-visible sampling regressions. This doc is a draft; thumbs up to formalize as a canary checklist and add to rollout gating for quantized models.
